name: Kang-Petrov Arms KPS-12D 'Typhoon'
description:
The KPS-12D Typhoon is a high-capacity submachine gun built around a 75-round drum magazine that gives the weapon its distinctive profile. Chambered in 9mm caseless, the Typhoon fires at 1,100 rpm and can empty its drum in just over four seconds. The weapon exists for one purpose: sustained volume of fire from a man-portable platform.

Kang-Petrov made no attempt at subtlety with the Typhoon. The drum magazine protrudes from the bottom of the receiver, making concealment impossible. The weapon is heavy by SMG standards at 3.1 kilograms loaded. Accuracy beyond 30 meters is optimistic. But within its intended engagement envelope — close range, high volume, maximum suppression — the Typhoon is terrifyingly effective.

At Φ1,200, the Typhoon occupies a price point between the bargain-basement Rattler and professional-grade options. Its customers are operators who prioritize volume over precision: gang enforcers, untrained militia, and anyone whose tactical doctrine amounts to 'more bullets.' The weapon's simplicity means it rarely malfunctions, and the drum magazine provides enough rounds to compensate for poor marksmanship through statistical probability.
specifications:
caliber: 9mm caseless
effective_range: 50m
rate_of_fire: 1,100 rpm (cyclic)
magazine_capacity: 75 rounds (drum)
weight: 3.1 kg (loaded)
tactical_use: The Typhoon's tactical role is suppression through volume. Its 75-round drum and high cyclic rate allow a single operator to lay down continuous fire that pins enemies behind cover and denies movement through kill zones. Accuracy is secondary — the weapon creates a wall of bullets rather than placing individual shots. In defensive scenarios, a Typhoon operator can hold a corridor or doorway against multiple attackers through sheer volume of fire.
cultural_context: The Typhoon is the weapon of overwhelming force applied without finesse. It is simultaneously feared and mocked — feared for the volume of fire it delivers, mocked for the lack of skill required to operate it. In street parlance, calling someone a 'Typhoon shooter' implies they compensate for incompetence with ammunition expenditure. Despite the stigma, the weapon sells in enormous quantities because its effectiveness does not require skill.
story_hooks: A building siege was broken by a single Typhoon operator who emptied four drums down a hallway in two minutes. The hallway was destroyed, but the attackers retreated. The operator is now deaf in one ear.
A modified Typhoon with a 150-round extended drum has appeared on the black market. The modification is crude but functional, and the weapon has been used in three mass-casualty events.

physical_description.visual_profile: A brutish, utilitarian submachine gun dominated by an enormous cylindrical drum magazine that bulges aggressively from beneath the receiver. The weapon has a compact, almost organic silhouette — wide and bottom-heavy, with a pronounced grip angle. It reads as deliberately unrefined, engineered for function over form.
physical_description.dimensions: Length: 38cm (stock collapsed), 42cm (stock extended); Width: 12cm at drum magazine; Height: 22cm (including drum); Barrel length: 12.7cm
physical_description.weight_description: Hefty and front-weighted when loaded — the drum magazine shifts the balance point noticeably downward. Feels substantial and purposeful in the hand, demanding respect through its mass.
physical_description.primary_material: Stamped steel receiver with polymer furniture; drum magazine is aluminum alloy with reinforced ribbing
physical_description.finish: Matte phosphate-coated steel on the receiver with brushed aluminum accents on the drum. Worn in appearance — the phosphate shows micro-scratches and slight surface oxidation suggesting field use rather than parade polish.
physical_description.color_scheme: Gunmetal gray body with the drum magazine in darker aluminum gray; accents of industrial black on the polymer handguard and charging handle
physical_description.grip_texture: Rubberized polymer grip with aggressive vertical ribbing for control; the magazine well has textured grip panels to assist loading and manipulation
distinctive_features: Oversized cylindrical drum magazine with radial cooling vents
Simplified blowback bolt carrier with exposed top charging handle
Minimalist iron sights (non-adjustable post and aperture)
Two stubby picatinny rails mounted on the receiver sides
Prominent heat vents along the barrel shroud
Kang-Petrov Arms logo stamped into the steel above the magazine well
Serial number plate with date-of-manufacture stamp
Slight carbon scoring around the muzzle and barrel shroud from sustained fire
Loose rattle when magazine is fully loaded — audible round count indicator
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: KANG-PETROV ARMS in Cyrillic and Latin script stamped into the left side of the receiver; KPS-12D engraved below the charging handle; manufacturer serial plate on the right side with holographic anti-counterfeiting thread
physical_description.condition_typical: Field-worn but functional. The phosphate coating shows honest use — scratches, minor dents, and discoloration from handling. Operators rarely maintain aesthetic condition; the weapon is expected to be dirty and scarred. The drum magazine often bears impact marks and improvised repair tape at seams.
